headline: Nuclear plants slow down as the Danube drops

sources.title: Record low Danube levels push some countries in Eastern Europe to the brink of energy emergency
Record low Danube levels prompt central European governments to take emergency action
Romania seeks to divert Danube water to keep Cernavoda nuclear power plant online

chunks.text: The Danube has fallen to its lowest level [[on record]], and the countries along it are [[short of]] electricity. In Budapest the river measured about 10 centimeters on Monday, August 3, 2026, well under the old record of 33 centimeters, set in 2018. Hungary's only nuclear plant stands beside the town of Paks, about 90 kilometers south of the [[capital]], and normally {{makes up}} about half of the country's electricity production. On Monday its four Soviet-built reactors had been {{cut back}} to 240 megawatts, [[compared with]] a normal 2,000. The Danube has been low before. What is new is that it has almost {{shut down}} a nuclear plant for the first time in 44 years.

chunks.text: The Paks plant uses Danube water to cool its reactors, so a low river means less power. To {{keep up with}} [[demand]], Hungary has asked everyone to use less. On Saturday the government {{brought in}} [[mandatory]] limits for large factories and shops, and asked families to save electricity between 5 and 10 in the evening, the hours of [[peak]] use. Electric freight trains cannot run in those hours, a step expected to save 70 to 90 megawatt hours a day. Prime Minister Péter Magyar said [[voluntary]] savings on Sunday cut demand by 700 megawatts, and that a full shutdown could still be {{put off}}, [[at least for now]].

chunks.text: Romania is in the same position. The [[flow]] of the Danube there has fallen to about 1,500 cubic meters a second, less than a third of the July [[average]]. One of the two 680 megawatt reactors at the Cernavoda plant has already stopped, and the other is running at about half [[capacity]]. Together they normally [[supply]] [[roughly]] a fifth of Romania's electricity. To {{hold back}} the water that escapes down a side channel called the Bala arm, and {{send it past}} the plant, more than 100 soldiers {{set off}} 180 kilograms of [[explosives]] at a rock formation there on Monday. The navy also plans to sink four barges carrying about 500 tons of stone across the same channel. Acting Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan declared a nationwide energy [[alert]] for August and {{turned to}} Ukraine for extra nuclear power. The carmakers Dacia and Ford have stopped production until August 19.

chunks.text: Serbia is feeling the same [[squeeze]]. Its two hydroelectric plants on the Danube, Djerdap I and Djerdap II, are running at 20 and 30 percent of capacity, and together they normally provide about 18 percent of the country's power. Prime Minister Djuro Macut held an emergency meeting and asked people to use air conditioning [[as little as possible]]. Slovakia's prime minister, Robert Fico, said his country was watching closely and was ready to {{step in}}. Daytime temperatures have {{gone up}} past 38 degrees Celsius, and the heat has not {{let up}} since May. Romania's energy ministry expects the hardest [[stretch]] to last until about August 15, but no real rain is [[forecast]] for weeks.
